source: Scene-locked vertical (Instagram) reel on John 1:1 (Evidence Library, Jesus tab, ev-s3 card 06 'John 1:1 and the Pre-existence of Christ'). POSITIVE CASE ONLY - no objection beat (the JW 'a god' reply stays in the essay/card). Wording PORTED from the certified card's 'The Case, Plainly' tier (was-not-began; with God = personally distinct, not another name for the Father; 'all things were made through him' puts the Word on the Maker's side of the line; 'two truths, held together, not one traded away for the other'; 17:5; 20:28; 'that Word became flesh, and lived among us') and library/john11.html. Deity/Trinity tier -> dual-consensus (argument + orthodoxy + neutrality). Calibration: 'fully shares the one divine nature' is grounded by John 1:3 context + the distinction clause, not asserted from the missing-article grammar alone (per john11.html stamp). Full humanity carried by 'the Word became flesh' (John 1:14). Per-scene dur ESTIMATED; render-intro.py rewrites them from the real speech length when voiced locally.
voiceover: Almost every story about Jesus starts where a life starts. The Gospel of John starts before the beginning of anything at all. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Who is the Word? A few lines later John tells us: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Word is Jesus of Nazareth. First, notice the verb. Of created things, John says they came to be. Of the Word, he says: was. When the beginning happened, the Word already was. Second: the Word was with God. Face-to-face with him, in relationship. The Word is personally distinct from the Father — not another name for him. Third: the Word was God. And three lines later, John says all things were made through him. The Word stands on the Maker's side of the line between Creator and creation — not among the things made. So John holds two truths together. Distinct from the Father. And fully sharing the one divine nature. Not one traded away for the other. And the rest of John says the same. Jesus prays for the glory that I had with you before the world existed. And Thomas, seeing the risen Jesus, says: My Lord and my God. In the beginning was the Word. The Word was God. And that Word became flesh, and lived among us. Read the full case — the Greek, the history, and the questions people ask — at apologiadaily.com.
